With a firmer FuelCell midsole and Energy Arc plate on a nimbler platform than the SC Elite, it is aimed at 5K to half-marathon racing and hard interval sessions. Runners who find 40mm super shoes squirmy will like its direct, connected feel.
pros: Excellent for 5K-10K racing and track-adjacent workouts
Lighter and more agile than max-stack racers
cons: Less protection for the full marathon
Firm ride is unforgiving on easy days

name: New Balance SC Rebel v1
description: The reboot of the Rebel franchise as the plated SuperComp training partner to the SC Elite v6: a 40mm Infinion foam stack with a propulsion plate at just 218g. RoadTrailRun's July 2026 multi-tester review calls it 'a Rebelation' for uptempo and long sessions; it releases August 20, 2026. It is a big price and geometry jump from the $140 unplated Rebel v5, which simpler-trainer fans may prefer while stock lasts.
pros: Bouncy 40mm Infinion stack with plate pop
Very light for its stack (7.7 oz)
Versatile from daily miles to race-adjacent workouts
cons: Low 4mm drop and plate won't suit everyone

name: New Balance SC Trainer v3
description: The SC Trainer v3 is the training partner to the SC Elite: a high-stack FuelCell shoe with an Energy Arc carbon plate built to survive daily mileage. It trades some of the racer's aggression for a more stable platform and a durable outsole. Best for long runs and uptempo days when you want plated assistance without burning race shoes.
pros: Plated super-trainer ride at trainer durability
Protective high stack for long runs
More stable than the racing version

name: Nike Alphafly 3
description: The Alphafly 3 is Nike's flagship marathon racer, combining a full carbon Flyplate, ZoomX foam, and dual forefoot Air Zoom pods on a continuous single-piece midsole. It was the shoe under Kelvin Kiptum's world record and remains one of the most propulsive long-distance racers available. The tall, springy platform rewards rhythmical midfoot striking and is strictly a race-day tool.
pros: Propulsive Air pods plus carbon plate
More stable and smoother than Alphafly 2
cons: Ride is too specialized for training

name: Nike Alphafly 4
description: The Alphafly 4 continues Nike's max-tech marathon racer formula: ZoomX foam, a full-length carbon Flyplate, and forefoot Air Zoom units at the 40mm legal limit. Expect the same aggressive, bouncy propulsion as the 3 with updated geometry and upper. It exists for one job, racing 10K to the marathon as fast as possible.
cons: Not durable enough for regular training

name: Nike Downshifter 13
description: The Downshifter 13 is Nike's entry-level running shoe, with simple EVA cushioning and a breathable mesh upper at a budget price. It works for new runners logging short, easy miles and doubles as a gym or walking shoe. The basic foam and modest stack mean experienced runners will outgrow it quickly.
pros: Fine for gym and casual miles
cons: Not built for high mileage or long runs

name: Nike Downshifter 14
description: The Downshifter 14 updates Nike's budget staple with a refreshed upper over the same simple EVA midsole formula. It remains a starter shoe for casual runners, walkers, and gym-goers who want the swoosh under $100. Serious mileage calls for a Winflo or Pegasus instead.
pros: Versatile for gym and casual use
cons: Durability and cushioning limits for real training

name: Nike Interact Run
description: A budget trainer notable as Nike's first sub-$100 shoe with a plush Flyknit upper, riding on a modest foam midsole. Good for newer runners doing casual weekly miles who want a shoe that doubles for everyday wear. Skip it if you need real cushioning for long runs, strong traction, or stability features.
pros: Great step-in comfort for the price

name: Nike Journey Run
description: A value-focused daily trainer with a wide, planted base that RunRepeat rates as exceptional value with rock-solid stability. Best for beginners and budget-minded runners doing short, easy runs that also want an everyday shoe. The midsole runs firmer than expected and the sharply tapered toe box will bother wide-footed runners; it's not the shoe for long distances or speed work.
cons: Not for long runs or speed work

name: Nike Pegasus 41
description: Nike's flagship daily trainer moved to full-length ReactX foam with dual Air Zoom units in the 41, giving a snappier, slightly softer ride than the 40. It remains the do-everything workhorse for easy miles, tempo days, and long runs alike. Not the plushest or the fastest shoe in the lineup, but it fits most feet and rarely misses.
pros: ReactX foam is bouncier than past Pegasus foam
cons: Not exciting for dedicated speed work

name: Nike Pegasus 42
description: The latest Pegasus keeps the ReactX midsole and dual Air Zoom units of the 41 with a refined upper and small fit tweaks. It stays true to the line's identity: a durable, moderately cushioned daily trainer that handles everything from easy days to steady long runs. Runners wanting maximum softness or a super-light ride should look elsewhere in Nike's range.

name: Nike Pegasus Plus
description: Essentially the successor to the Pegasus Turbo, the Pegasus Plus pairs a full-length ZoomX midsole with a stripped-down Flyknit upper. It is a light, energetic trainer that livens up uptempo days and shorter races without a plate. The thin upper and price put it in enthusiast territory rather than everyday-value territory.
pros: Full ZoomX ride at a trainer height
Light and versatile for tempo work
cons: ZoomX outsole coverage wears faster than the standard Pegasus

name: Nike Pegasus Plus 2
description: The second Pegasus Plus continues the formula of full-length ZoomX foam in a light, plate-free trainer built for faster daily miles. Expect the same energetic, flexible ride as the original with an updated upper for a more secure lockdown. It sits between the standard Pegasus and Nike's plated speed shoes in both feel and price.

name: Nike Pegasus Premium
description: The Pegasus Premium stacks ZoomX, a full-length sculpted Air Zoom unit, and ReactX into the tallest, bounciest Pegasus ever made. The ride is fun and highly cushioned for long cruisy miles, but all that tech makes it noticeably heavy. It is a max-stack experience shoe, not a racer, and the price reflects the tech rather than pure performance.
pros: Visible full-length Air Zoom gives a lively ride

name: Nike Quest 6
description: The Quest 6 slots just above the Revolution in Nike's budget range, adding a bit more midsole and a more structured upper for everyday easy running. It is a serviceable, no-frills trainer for beginners and low-mileage runners. The foam is plain EVA, so the ride is firm and utilitarian rather than plush or springy.
pros: Secure fit for a budget shoe

name: Nike Revolution 7
description: The Revolution 7 is Nike's cheapest running shoe, a soft-ish EVA cruiser aimed at beginners, walkers, and everyday wear. It is comfortable enough for short easy runs and is one of the best-selling shoes in the world on price alone. There is no advanced foam or structure here, and it shows on longer or faster efforts.
pros: Comfortable for walking and short runs

name: Nike Revolution 8
description: Nike's entry-level budget trainer with a simple foam midsole and a light, flexible build. A sensible pick for beginners, walk-run programs, and short easy miles on a tight budget. Runners logging serious weekly mileage or wanting any bounce should spend up to a Winflo or Pegasus.
pros: Works as an everyday casual sneaker
cons: Not built for long runs or speed work

name: Nike Streakfly 2
description: The Streakfly 2 is Nike's short-distance road racer, a featherweight ZoomX shoe built for the 5K and 10K where ground feel and turnover beat max stack. A midfoot plate adds some snap without the stiffness of a full carbon racer. It is a specialist: fantastic for short races and intervals, undercushioned for most runners beyond 10K.
cons: Too little cushion for long races
Niche use case for the price

name: Nike Structure 26
description: The Structure 26 is Nike's traditional stability trainer, using a firmer medial midsole and a wide, guided platform to keep overpronators tracking straight. Updated foam softens the ride compared with older Structures while keeping the supportive character. It is the Nike answer to the Adrenaline GTS and GT-2000 for runners who need real medial support.
cons: Heavier and stiffer than neutral peers
Support feel is unnecessary for neutral runners

name: Nike Structure Plus
description: The Structure Plus brings Nike's premium-foam treatment to its stability line, pairing a taller, softer midsole with a wide guided base and medial support. It targets overpronators who want max-cushion comfort for long and easy miles instead of the firmer standard Structure. As a Plus-tier shoe it carries extra weight and a higher price.

name: Nike Vaporfly 4
description: The Vaporfly 4 trims weight from an already legendary racer, pairing ZoomX foam with a full carbon plate in a lower, nimbler package than the Alphafly. It is arguably the most versatile super shoe Nike makes, at home from 5K to the marathon and light enough for hard workouts. The narrow racing fit and thin upper are all business.
cons: Narrow fit will not suit wide feet

name: Nike Vomero 18
description: The Vomero 18 grew into a true max-cushion trainer, stacking soft ZoomX over a stable ReactX base at 46mm in the heel. It delivers one of the best plush-ride values on the market at $150, ideal for recovery days, easy miles, and heavier runners who want protection. It is not light or fast, and it does not pretend to be.
pros: ZoomX over ReactX is soft yet stable
cons: Too much shoe for speed work

name: Nike Vomero Plus
description: The Vomero Plus swaps the standard model's dual-foam stack for full-length ZoomX, making it the softest and bounciest shoe in the Vomero family. It is a plush cruiser for long runs and easy days that still feels lively thanks to the all-ZoomX midsole. Softness comes at the cost of some inherent stability, so runners who need a steadier platform may prefer the Vomero 18 or 19.
pros: Full ZoomX midsole is soft and bouncy
cons: Soft platform can feel unstable in corners
ZoomX midsole durability is only average

name: Nike Vomero Premium
description: Nike's tallest trainer, the Vomero Premium piles ZoomX and large Zoom Air units into a towering max-stack platform aimed at ultimate long-run comfort. The ride is enormous, soft, and surprisingly bouncy, but the shoe is heavy and the price is steep. It is for runners who want the most cushioning Nike sells and do not care about the scale.
pros: Bouncy Air-assisted ride for its size
cons: Too tall and soft for faster running

name: Nike Winflo 11
description: The Winflo 11 is Nike's mid-budget daily trainer, combining Cushlon foam with a full-length Air Zoom unit for a firm but smooth ride. It covers easy miles reliably and holds up well for the price. The foam is basic compared with ReactX or ZoomX, so it suits newer runners and value shoppers more than performance seekers.

name: Nike Winflo 12
description: The Winflo 12 continues the line's role as Nike's dependable budget-plus trainer, with cushioned foam, a full-length Air Zoom unit, and a refreshed upper. It is built for everyday easy running and gym-to-road versatility rather than performance. A sensible pick for runners who want a real running shoe without flagship pricing.

name: Nike Zoom Fly 6
description: The Zoom Fly 6 is Nike's super trainer: a ZoomX core wrapped in a firmer SR-02 carrier with a full carbon Flyplate. It gives much of the plated race-day feel in a more durable, more stable package for tempo runs, marathon-pace work, and even racing on a budget. Heavier than a true super shoe, it is the training partner to the Vaporfly rather than a replacement.
pros: Carbon-plated ride at a trainer price

name: On Cloudboom Max
description: A glass-fiber Speedboard marathon shoe aimed squarely at 4:00-5:00 finishers who want stability over bounce. The dual-density Helion HF ride is firm, stiff, and heavy for anything labeled race day, and reviewers found little energy return. Skip it if you want a lively super shoe; consider it only for a stable, controlled platform over long, steady miles.
pros: Very stable for a high-stack race shoe
Breathable upper with secure heel hold
cons: Heavy for race day at 10.4 oz
Stiff, blocky ride with little pop
Some testers got rubbing and blisters

name: On Cloudboom Strike
description: On's full-length carbon super shoe with a tall Helion HF PEBA midsole, worn to major marathon wins. The ride is soft and rockered with a snug, race-specific fit. It rewards efficient midfoot strikers more than heel strikers.
pros: Soft, fast PEBA and carbon setup

name: On Cloudboom Strike 2
description: The second generation of On's carbon-plated marathon racer, keeping the tall Helion HF PEBA stack and aggressive rocker of the original. Expect small refinements to the upper and geometry rather than a rework. Still a snug-fitting shoe aimed at efficient racers.

name: On Cloudboom Strike 2 LightSpray
description: The robot-sprayed laceless version of On's marathon racer, sharing the new CloudTec Sphere midsole, updated Helion HF foam, and curved Speedboard with the standard Strike 2 while dropping to 158 g. It launched July 30, 2026 at $310 for racers chasing every gram. The one-piece upper fits snug with zero adjustability, so fit-sensitive runners should stick with the laced version.
pros: New Helion HF foam is 15% lighter than the prior generation

name: On Cloudboom Strike LightSpray
description: The Cloudboom Strike platform topped with On's robot-sprayed, laceless LightSpray upper, cutting the shoe to around 170 grams. It is one of the lightest marathon super shoes available, with the same carbon plate and Helion HF foam underneath. The minimal upper fits like a sock and offers little adjustability.
pros: Exceptionally light for a marathon shoe
Same fast plate and foam as the Strike
cons: No laces means no fit adjustment

name: On Cloudeclipse
description: On's max-cushion daily trainer with a double layer of CloudTec Phase pods and a Speedboard for structure. The ride is soft yet surprisingly stable thanks to the wide base, making it a strong pick for long easy miles. One of the more accessible-feeling shoes On makes.
pros: Handles long runs and recovery days well

name: On Cloudflow 5
description: A firm, stable lightweight trainer that On pitches at tempo days and fartleks. Build quality and lockdown are excellent, but lab testing measured very low energy return and it runs warm and heavy for a speed shoe. Best for runners who like a firm, connected ride; soft-foam fans should look elsewhere.
pros: Secure, premium upper with great lockdown
cons: Very firm with low energy return
Heavy and warm for a tempo shoe

name: On Cloudmonster 2
description: On's biggest CloudTec trainer, with oversized Helion-foam pods and a pronounced rocker for easy and long miles. It rides softer and smoother than the original but stays on the heavy side for a daily shoe. Best for runners who want a protective cruiser rather than anything fast.
pros: Smooth rockered ride for long miles

name: On Cloudmonster 3
description: The third generation of On's max-pod cruiser keeps the big CloudTec elements and rocker geometry while trimming a little weight. It remains a protective, smooth daily and long-run shoe rather than a fast one. A safe update for Cloudmonster fans.
cons: Still heavy for a daily trainer

name: On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper
description: On's plateless super trainer stacks a Helion HF PEBA top layer over a CloudTec EVA base with a big rockered profile. It covers daily miles, long runs, and uptempo work, and it is the sensible pick over the $280 LightSpray version, which shares the same midsole. The thin heel collar and pronounced medial arch will bother some runners, so try before buying if you are sensitive there.
pros: Versatile from easy miles to workouts
Same ride as the LightSpray version for $60 less
cons: Minimal heel collar padding can rub
Runs firm compared to plated super trainers

name: On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper LightSpray
description: A premium super-trainer that pairs the Cloudmonster Hyper's PEBA-based Helion HF midsole with On's robot-sprayed LightSpray upper. The one-piece upper cuts weight but offers minimal structure, so it suits efficient runners on uptempo long runs. Very expensive for a trainer.
pros: Very light for its cushion level
cons: Minimal upper structure won't suit everyone

name: On Cloudmonster Hyper
description: A super-trainer take on the Cloudmonster with a PEBA-based Helion HF midsole and no plate. It is noticeably bouncier and lighter than the standard Cloudmonster, suiting uptempo long runs and marathon-pace work. Pricey for a plateless trainer.
pros: Much lighter than the regular Cloudmonster

name: On Cloudrunner 2
description: A supportive, budget-friendlier On daily trainer with a wide base and gentle guidance elements rather than a firm medial post. Helion foam and CloudTec pods give a moderate, slightly firm ride that favors durability over excitement. A sensible pick for newer runners who want light support.

name: On Cloudrunner 3
description: A light-stability daily trainer with a plush upper, plastic heel clip, and raised sidewalls over a notably firm midsole. It suits beginners and stability seekers logging easy road miles who value a locked-in, controlled feel. Reviewers found the foam brick-like with little energy return and pointed to better value at or below its $160 price.
pros: Effective light stability without a harsh post
Full rubber outsole grips and wears well
cons: Weak value versus similarly priced rivals

name: On Cloudsurfer 2
description: On's softest everyday trainer, built on collapsing CloudTec Phase pods and Helion foam rather than firm rubber-feeling pods of older Ons. The ride is smooth and gentle, better for cruising and recovery days than picking up the pace. Light for how cushioned it feels.

name: On Cloudsurfer 3
description: The third version of On's soft CloudTec Phase daily trainer, continuing the smooth, collapsing-pod ride of its predecessors. It stays a comfort-first shoe for easy miles and recovery days. Expect modest refinements to the upper and foam rather than a redesign.

name: On Cloudsurfer Max
description: The max-stack version of the Cloudsurfer, stacking more CloudTec Phase foam under a rockered platform. It delivers a plush, smooth ride for long easy runs and recovery days. Heavier and more expensive than the standard Cloudsurfer without adding versatility.
cons: Noticeably heavier than the regular Cloudsurfer

name: On Cloudsurfer Next
description: A slightly cheaper, lighter spin-off of the Cloudsurfer with the same CloudTec Phase midsole concept. It is a comfortable, unfussy daily trainer that leans soft and smooth over energetic. A good entry point to On's running line.
cons: Ride can feel flat at faster paces

name: Puma Deviate Nitro 3
description: A carbon-composite-plated super trainer with Nitro Elite foam that handles daily miles, long runs, and workouts alike. The PWRPLATE gives it snap without making the ride harsh at easy paces. One of the most versatile one-shoe-quiver options at its price.
pros: Plated pop at a fair price

name: Puma Deviate Nitro 4
description: The fourth Deviate Nitro continues the plated super-trainer formula with Nitro Elite foam and a PWRPLATE for versatile training. It remains a strong single-shoe option covering easy days through tempo work. Expect refinement over revolution versus version 3.
pros: Good value for a plated shoe
cons: Not as light as dedicated speed shoes

name: Puma Deviate Nitro Elite 3
description: Puma's more traditional carbon racer, with Nitro Elite foam and a full-length PWRPLATE in a lighter, less extreme package than the Fast-R. It is fast, relatively stable for a super shoe, and priced below most flagship racers. A strong pick from 5K to the marathon.
pros: Light and fast without extreme geometry
cons: Slightly less bounce than top-tier racers

name: Puma Deviate Nitro Elite 4
description: The fourth Deviate Nitro Elite keeps Puma's approachable carbon-racer formula: Nitro Elite foam, a full PWRPLATE, and a manageable geometry. It targets racers who want super-shoe speed without the instability of more extreme designs. Expect incremental foam and upper updates.
pros: Competitive price for a super shoe

name: Puma Deviate Pure Nitro
description: A plate-free, PEBA-based lightweight trainer built to chase the Adidas Adizero Evo SL at a lower price. At roughly 7.6 oz over a 38 mm heel it disappears on daily miles and strides, though reviewers found the foam flatter than its specs suggest. Buy it for the weight, fit, and grip rather than for propulsion at hard paces.
pros: Comfortable true-to-size upper with roomy toe box

name: Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 2
description: Puma's split-sole marathon racer with an exposed carbon PWRPLATE and Nitro Elite foam in a decoupled two-part midsole. The aggressive geometry drives strong forward roll for efficient racers. It ran on many podiums but is heavier than the best in class.

name: Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3
description: A computationally redesigned version of the Fast-R that stripped roughly two ounces from its predecessor while keeping the exposed carbon plate and Nitro Elite foam. Lab and race results made it one of the most talked-about marathon shoes of 2025. Very expensive and unapologetically race-only.
cons: One of the priciest racers on the market
Extreme design isn't for everyday runners

name: Puma ForeverRun Nitro 2
description: Puma's stability trainer, using a firmer Nitro foam frame around a softer core plus raised sidewalls instead of an old-school medial post. It guides the foot without feeling intrusive, making it a good pick for overpronators and heavier mileage. Solid rather than exciting.

name: Puma ForeverRun Nitro 3
description: The third generation of Puma's stability trainer moves to a dual-density PEBA-blend NITROFOAM midsole on a new, wider last, pairing a soft nitrogen-infused core with a firmer supportive rim. It keeps the unobtrusive, non-medial-post approach to guidance that made the line a sleeper stability pick, built to hold up over roughly 500 miles of daily training.
pros: Guidance without a stiff medial post
Durable dual-density foam rated for high mileage
cons: Too new for independent long-term durability data
Stability-focused ride lacks pop for faster work

name: Puma MagMax Nitro
description: Puma's first true max-stack trainer piles deep NitroFoam under a wide, stable platform with near-total PumaGrip coverage. It shines for long easy miles, recovery days, and heavier runners or heel strikers who want shock absorption over agility. It is on the heavy side with modest energy return, so keep it away from speed days.
pros: Very stable for its stack height
Fair price for a max trainer

name: Puma MagMax Nitro 2
description: The second MagMax trims about half an ounce, reworks the outsole, and keeps the huge 46 mm NitroFoam stack, earning strong reviews as a do-it-all max-cushion trainer. It stays composed from recovery pace through steady uptempo running and works well for bigger runners. The midfoot runs narrow and the ride leans firm-for-max, so plush-foam seekers may be disappointed.
cons: Not as soft as some max-cushion rivals

name: Puma Magnify Nitro 2
description: Puma's max-cushion cruiser stacks a thick slab of Nitro foam for soft, protective easy miles. It suits recovery days and bigger runners who want plushness with dependable PumaGrip traction. Too heavy and soft for anything resembling speed.
pros: Good value for a max-cushion shoe

name: Puma Velocity Nitro 3
description: One of the best value daily trainers around, with nitrogen-infused Nitro foam and grippy PumaGrip rubber for well under most rivals' prices. The ride is balanced and reliable for everything from easy days to moderate long runs. Nothing flashy, just a workhorse.
cons: Ride is merely decent, not exciting

name: Puma Velocity Nitro 4
description: The fourth Velocity Nitro adds a touch more foam while keeping the line's honest daily-trainer character and excellent PumaGrip traction. It stays one of the strongest value picks in running shoes. A do-everything trainer for runners who don't want to overthink it.
pros: Comfortable for a range of runs

name: Reebok Floatride Energy 6
description: The long-running value trainer continues with firm, dependable Floatride Energy foam and a nylon X-plate for mild snap and stability. A practical, durable choice for budget-minded daily miles. Runners wanting soft or springy cushioning for long runs should look elsewhere.

name: Reebok FloatZig 1
description: Reebok's return to serious running, pairing Floatride Energy foam with a zig-zag geometry midsole and outsole. It is a fun, well-priced neutral daily trainer that earned surprisingly strong reviews for its smooth, lively ride.
pros: Lively Floatride Energy foam at a fair price
cons: Modest stack offers less long-run protection

name: Reebok FloatZig 2
description: The FloatZig sequel drops to $120 while adding softer SuperFloat+ foam, making it one of the best budget daily trainers of 2025. Great for easy and recovery miles with a roomy fit and retro looks. Wet-road traction and tempo work are its weak spots.
cons: Wet traction issues from open Zig outsole
Not a tempo or long-run shoe

name: Reebok FloatZig Symmetros
description: The supportive, higher-spec sibling to the FloatZig 1, launched the same day with a firmer, well-structured 33/27mm platform. Suits runners who want gentle support and a planted feel rather than soft bounce. Firm-shoe skeptics and speed seekers should pass.

name: Reebok FloatZig X1
description: Reebok's budget-friendly carbon-plated racer: a full-length plate in a firm-but-bouncy 33/27mm package at $200. It suits runners who find max-stack super shoes unstable and like a natural heel-to-toe roll. Those wanting plush super-foam bounce will find it firm and it needs a 20-mile break-in.

name: Salomon Aero Blaze 3
description: Light, low-slung daily trainer with a soft, energetic ride that handles everything from recovery pace to tempo. Good value at $140 and light for its stack. Heavier runners may bottom out the midsole and wide feet will find it too narrow.
pros: Fun, energetic ride at a fair price
Light for the cushion on offer
cons: Wet grip is mediocre in the forefoot

name: Salomon Aero Glide 2
description: No-frills max-cushion daily trainer with Salomon's Energy Foam. Stable and very durable for easy miles, but the ride is rigid and short on energy return next to similarly priced rivals. Fine as a mileage workhorse; skip it for anything lively.

name: Salomon Aero Glide 3
description: Salomon's max-cushion road cruiser with a tall slab of energyFOAM and a gently rockered ride. It is built for easy miles and long runs where comfort matters more than pace, with a wide base that keeps the high stack stable.
pros: Plush, protective cushioning for long easy miles
cons: Too much shoe for uptempo days

name: Salomon Aero Glide 4
description: The 2026 update to Salomon's max-cushion road trainer keeps the tall energyFOAM stack and rockered geometry while trimming a little weight and refining the upper. It remains an easy-day and long-run shoe for runners who want protection over pop.
pros: High, protective stack for recovery and long runs
cons: Salomon road shoes have limited retail presence in the US

name: Salomon S/Lab Phantasm 2
description: Salomon's carbon-plated road marathon racer, pairing a supercritical PEBA-based foam with a full-length plate and an aggressive rocker. It is a legitimate super shoe from a brand better known for trail, with a firm, propulsive ride that rewards efficient form.
pros: Light and aggressive at race pace
cons: Narrow fit will not suit wide feet

name: Salomon S/Lab Phantasm 3
description: Salomon's elite marathon super shoe, 38 g lighter than the Phantasm 2, with soft optiFOAM+ PEBA, an energyBLADE carbon plate, and an aero gaiter upper. Fast, bouncy and surprisingly stable, but it only comes alive at genuinely quick paces. Narrow Salomon fit and a fiddly step-in make it a poor pick for casual racers.
pros: Soft, bouncy PEBA with real stability
cons: Needs fast paces and a midfoot strike to shine

name: Salomon S/Lab Spectur
description: A carbon-plated marathon shoe deliberately built for 3-hour-plus finishers: winged plate, wide stable platform, and forgiving PEBA-over-EVA stack. Bouncy and fun without the tippiness of elite racers. Faster runners chasing maximum aggression should race in something else.
pros: Super-shoe tech tuned for everyday marathoners
cons: Heavy next to elite carbon racers

name: Salomon Spectur 2
description: Uptempo trainer with a glass-fiber Energy Blade plate and a smooth rocker, positioned as the training partner to the S/Lab racers. Solid and balanced for tempo runs and intervals. It is middle-of-the-road against the Mach 6 and Endorphin Speed class, so shop the competition first.
pros: Smooth plated rocker at a reasonable price

name: Saucony Endorphin Azura
description: A brand-new plateless supertrainer: full PWRRUN PB superfoam with SpeedRoll geometry that delivers a snappy, efficient ride at all paces for $150. Great for uptempo workouts and daily miles for runners who want superfoam bounce without a plate, and surprisingly stable for the category. Skip it if you want a soft, squishy ride (it runs firm) or if a tapered forefoot bothers your toes.
pros: Responsive PWRRUN PB ride at every pace
Very stable for a superfoam shoe
cons: Aggressive forefoot taper can crowd toes

name: Saucony Endorphin Elite 2
description: Saucony's no-compromise flagship racer, built on an aggressive slotted carbon plate and the brand's softest, highest-rebound foam (PWRRUN HG). It's tuned purely for marathon race day, with a propulsive forward tip that rewards committed, fast running. Overkill for training and too aggressive for easy miles.
pros: Very light for a max-stack racer
cons: Unstable and inefficient at slower paces

name: Saucony Endorphin Elite 3
description: The third-generation Elite, due August 2026, continues Saucony's top-of-the-line marathon racer with PWRRUN HG foam and an aggressive carbon plate at the maximum legal stack. Expect small weight and geometry refinements aimed at elite and serious amateur marathoners. Strictly a race-day tool.
pros: Built purely for fast marathon racing
cons: Too aggressive for most training runs

name: Saucony Endorphin Pro 4
description: Saucony's carbon-plated marathon racer, stacking a PWRRUN HG topsole over PWRRUN PB with a full-length carbon plate and SPEEDROLL geometry. The ride is firmer and more stable than the bounciest super shoes, which many runners prefer late in a marathon. A dependable racer from 10K to the marathon.
pros: More forgiving than most carbon racers for heel strikers
cons: Snug racing fit isn't for wide feet

name: Saucony Endorphin Pro 5
description: The 2026 update to Saucony's carbon racer pushes the stack toward the legal limit and softens the PWRRUN PB and PWRRUN HG combination for more bounce. It keeps the carbon plate and SPEEDROLL rocker that make the Pro line efficient over the full marathon. A more forgiving, modern super shoe than the Pro 4.
pros: Bouncier, taller ride than the Pro 4
cons: Narrow fit and tall stack demand a settled stride

name: Saucony Endorphin Speed 4
description: The benchmark plated super-trainer: a PWRRUN PB midsole with a flexible winged nylon plate and SPEEDROLL rocker. It's fast enough to race, forgiving enough for daily training, and remains one of the most versatile shoes in running. If you own one fast shoe that isn't a carbon racer, this is the default answer.
pros: Outstanding versatility from tempo to race day
Bouncy PEBA foam with a forgiving nylon plate
Light for how much shoe you get
cons: Jack of all trades, master of none
Upper runs slightly roomy for racing

name: Saucony Endorphin Speed 5
description: The current Endorphin Speed sticks with PWRRUN PB and the winged nylon plate while trimming weight and dialing in the fit. It remains the do-it-all workout shoe for runners who want super-shoe feel without super-shoe fragility or price. Handles tempos, intervals, long runs, and racing when you don't want a stiff carbon plate.
pros: Lighter and better-fitting than the Speed 4
cons: Not as explosive as a true carbon racer

name: Saucony Endorphin Trainer
description: A carbon-plated max-stack trainer built on IncrediRun foam that never figured out what it wants to be: too heavy for speedwork, too dense and blocky for recovery days. Reviewers found the plate purposeless and the ride bricky despite the bouncy top layer of foam. Only worth a look for runners who specifically like firm, dense plated trainers, especially at closeout prices.
cons: Heavy and blocky for a plated trainer
Plate adds little; awkward in-between ride
Sparse outsole rubber and loud footstrike

name: Saucony Guide 17
description: A light-touch stability trainer that dropped the medial post for CenterPath geometry, a wide base with raised sidewalls that guides the foot rather than correcting it. Great for mild overpronators who hate clunky stability shoes. Runners who need firm, structured support, or a precise fit, should look elsewhere, because it runs a bit long.
pros: Lighter and more nimble than most stability trainers
cons: Runs large; consider a half size down
Support too subtle for severe overpronators

name: Saucony Guide 18
description: The stability sibling of the Ride, using a PWRRUN+ midsole with Saucony's CenterPath geometry: a wide base, raised sidewalls, and subtle guidance instead of a hard medial post. It supports overpronators without feeling stiff or corrective. A friendly pick for runners who want unobtrusive support for daily miles.
pros: Works for neutral runners who like a stable base
cons: Not much energy return for faster days

name: Saucony Guide 19
description: The 2026 version of Saucony's long-running stability trainer, continuing the CenterPath guidance approach with PWRRUN+ foam on a broad, stable platform. It's built for overpronators and heel strikers who want structured daily mileage. Expect an evolution of the Guide 18 rather than a redesign.
cons: Modest update over the previous version

name: Saucony Hurricane 24
description: The revived Hurricane is a max-cushion stability tank: a PWRRUN PB core inside a supportive frame with CenterPath sidewalls on a very wide base. Excellent for overpronators and bigger runners logging easy miles who want deep cushioning plus real guidance. At 10.6 oz it is strictly a cruiser, so skip it if you want anything lively.
cons: Stiff, bulky feel at anything but easy paces

name: Saucony Hurricane 25
description: Saucony's premium max-cushion stability shoe, pairing a PWRRUN PB core with a firmer PWRRUN frame and CenterPath geometry for real guidance without a rigid post. It gives overpronators a plush, planted platform for daily and long miles. A strong pick for bigger runners who need both cushion and support.
cons: Feels ponderous at anything faster than easy pace

name: Saucony Hurricane 26
description: The 2026 Hurricane continues the formula of a soft PWRRUN PB core inside a supportive frame with CenterPath guidance. It's Saucony's flagship stability trainer for runners who want maximum cushion and structure in one shoe. Released mid-2026 as an incremental refinement of the Hurricane 25.
pros: Built to last under bigger runners
cons: One of the heavier trainers in the lineup

name: Saucony Kinvara 15
description: The long-running lightweight trainer that keeps things simple: PWRRUN foam, a 4mm drop, and very little else. It rewards efficient midfoot strikers who want a light, flexible shoe for daily miles and up-tempo days without plates or gimmicks. Minimal outsole rubber keeps weight down but limits durability.
pros: Good value for a lightweight trainer

name: Saucony Kinvara 16
description: A return to the classic Kinvara formula: light, flexible, low-stack, 4 mm drop, and very breathable. Fun for uptempo days and runners who like feeling the ground or building foot strength. The plain PWRRUN foam feels dated next to modern superfoam trainers, durability is mediocre, and the narrow fit will not work for wide feet.
pros: Classic low-drop ground feel at a fair price
cons: Low energy return from dated foam

name: Saucony Omni 22
description: A traditional moderate-stability workhorse using firm PWRRUN foam and a HOLLOW-TECH support unit: durable, planted, and smooth, but short on energy return. A sensible pick for overpronators and flat-footed runners who want structured support at a fair price. Runners chasing a lively or plush ride should look elsewhere.

name: Saucony Paramount Max
description: Saucony's new max-cushion recovery trainer built on ultra-soft IncrediRun foam: marshmallow plush, surprisingly light for its 43 mm bulk, and stable thanks to a wide platform. Built for recovery days and easy miles with a roomy, wide-foot-friendly fit. It is one-dimensional at $200: do not buy it hoping to pick up the pace.
pros: Roomy fit that suits wide feet
cons: Pricey at $200 versus more versatile trainers
Heel collar can rub with low socks

name: Saucony Ride 17
description: A soft-but-stable neutral daily trainer whose switch to a full PWRRUN+ midsole made it plusher (and nearly an ounce heavier) than the Ride 16. Good for easy miles and relaxed long runs on a wide, steady platform. Runners wanting a light, snappy do-everything trainer will find it sluggish.
pros: Wide platform is stable for a neutral shoe

name: Saucony Ride 18
description: Saucony's core neutral daily trainer, running a full PWRRUN+ TPU-bead midsole that is softer and bouncier than the old Ride formula. It handles easy miles, moderate long runs, and everyday training without drama. A safe, versatile first shoe for most runners.
pros: PWRRUN+ midsole is durable and lively
cons: Not fast enough for real workouts
Some rivals feel more exciting at this price

name: Saucony Ride 19
description: The 2026 update to Saucony's workhorse neutral trainer, keeping the PWRRUN+ midsole and balanced 8mm-drop platform with a refined upper. It stays true to the Ride formula: one shoe that covers most of a training week. Nothing flashy, just dependable daily mileage.
cons: Not a workout or race shoe

name: Saucony Tempus 2
description: A rare thing: a genuinely fast stability shoe. The Tempus 2 wraps a bouncy PWRRUN PB core in a supportive PWRRUN frame that guides the foot without a plate or a post. It lets overpronators pick up the pace in a shoe that still protects their stride, and plenty of neutral runners like it too.
pros: PEBA core gives real energy return
Works for neutral and overpronating runners alike
cons: Frame can feel firm underfoot at easy paces

name: Saucony Triumph 22
description: Saucony's plush neutral cruiser gained a full PWRRUN PB superfoam midsole, giving it a squishier, bouncier ride for easy and long days. The wide platform keeps all that softness stable, and the price held at $160. It is a one-pace shoe: comfortable and protective, but too heavy and warm for uptempo work.
pros: Stable wide platform for a max-cushion shoe
cons: Limited to easy and recovery paces

name: Saucony Triumph 23
description: Saucony's premium max-cushion neutral trainer, notable for moving to a full PEBA-based PWRRUN PB midsole, putting race-shoe foam in a plush daily package. It delivers a soft, bouncy ride for long runs and recovery days while staying reasonably light for its stack. One of the more energetic plush trainers on the market.
pros: PEBA-based foam is soft and springy
cons: High 10mm drop won't suit forefoot strikers

name: Saucony Triumph 24
description: The newest Triumph keeps the full PWRRUN PB midsole that transformed the line and refines the upper and outsole. It remains Saucony's plushest neutral trainer, aimed at long runs, high mileage, and runners who want a soft but lively ride. Freshly released for mid-2026.
cons: Too soft and tall for fast workouts

name: Skechers Aero Burst
description: The cushioned pillar of Skechers' performance-focused Aero line, with a tall Hyper Burst Ice midsole for soft, high-mileage comfort. It targets easy days and long runs, undercutting most max-cushion competitors on price.
pros: Soft, high-stack cushioning at a value price

name: Skechers Aero Razor
description: The Razor name returns inside the Aero line as a light, unplated speed trainer built on Hyper Burst foam. Like past Razors it is a workout specialist that efficient runners can also use as a fast daily shoe.
pros: Continues the well-loved Razor speed-shoe lineage
Light, snappy ride without a plate
cons: Not cushioned enough for long easy miles

name: Skechers Aero Spark
description: The lightweight trainer of the Aero line, using Hyper Burst foam in a lower, nimbler package for uptempo daily running. It suits runners who want one affordable shoe for everyday miles, strides, and faster sessions.
pros: Light and lively for the price

name: Skechers Aero Tempo
description: The plated speed shoe of the Aero line, combining Hyper Burst Ice foam with a stiffening plate for tempo runs and workouts. It plays the budget super-trainer role, giving plated pop well below the price of most competitors.
pros: Plated propulsion at a low price
cons: Less refined than premium super trainers
Fit runs a touch long for some

name: Skechers GOrun Razor 5
description: Bouncy lightweight tempo shoe with Hyperburst Pro foam, a carbon-infused forefoot H-plate, and a Goodyear outsole. Versatile as a fast daily trainer, workout shoe, or short-distance racer. The narrow toe box and loud styling are the main reasons to pass.
cons: Narrow toe box and snug midfoot

name: Topo Athletic Atmos 2
description: Topo's max-cushion road trainer gets softer in v2 with a 40/35mm ZipFoam stack, leaning into easy days, recovery miles, and all-day comfort. Great for runners wanting a broad-toe-box Bondi alternative. It lost some uptempo versatility, and its EVA-based foam is heavier than supercritical rivals.

name: Topo Athletic Cyclone 3
description: A 6.9 oz plateless speed shoe built on a single slab of supercritical PEBAX, functioning as a modern race flat for 5K-10K and interval days. Ideal for runners who want fast without carbon plates and with a real toe box. Not the shoe for easy miles or long-distance cushioning.
pros: Buttery soft upper with anatomical toe box
cons: Heel feels low at slow paces

name: Topo Athletic Magnifly 5
description: Topo's zero-drop road trainer stacks 30mm of ZipFoam under the whole foot, giving natural-running fans real cushioning without an offset. With its anatomical toe box and flexible forefoot, it's a direct, more padded alternative to the Altra Escalante.
pros: Anatomical toe box with secure midfoot

name: Topo Athletic Phantom 4
description: Topo's cushioned daily trainer gains 2mm of ZipFoam stack for a softer but not mushy ride. A dependable high-mileage cruiser for runners who want plush cushioning with a natural toe box and moderate 5mm drop. Runners chasing supercritical-foam bounce will find it a bit traditional.
cons: ZipFoam less lively than newer super foams

name: Topo Athletic Specter 2
description: Topo's plateless super-trainer runs a full Pebax midsole under an anatomical wide toe box and a low 5mm drop. It's a bouncy, versatile shoe that handles daily miles and uptempo work for runners who want performance foam without a cramped racing fit.
pros: Roomy toe box on a performance shoe
cons: No plate means less snap than racers
Fit runs generous for narrow feet

name: Topo Athletic Specter 3
description: The Specter 3 launches Topo's Pro Series as a 39mm, 7.7 oz unplated super trainer with bouncy A-TPU RevFoam and an aggressive rocker. Excellent for marathon-pace work and steady long runs for efficient neutral runners. Its narrow midfoot platform gets tippy at recovery paces.
pros: Very light for a 39mm super trainer
Versatile from daily miles to tempo

name: Topo Athletic Specter Elite
description: Topo's first carbon-plated super shoe pairs a full-length plate and A-TPU foam with the brand's signature wide, anatomical toe box, a rare combination in the racing category. It's bouncy without being mushy and rewards a longer rhythm, from 10K through the marathon, more than short, sharp efforts.
pros: Wide anatomic toe box unique among carbon super shoes
Very lightweight for a plated racer
Stable, wide base without feeling bulky
cons: Feels like a struggle at 5K-and-under efforts

name: Tracksmith Eliot Runner
description: Tracksmith's debut trainer: premium vintage-modern materials, a gum rubber outsole, and a firm traditional ride with a 10mm Pebax insole adding subtle pop. A style-first daily trainer for brand loyalists who also want it to work off the run. Runners chasing modern soft, bouncy foams or performance-per-dollar should look elsewhere, and sizing runs long.
cons: Firm, unexciting ride for the price

name: Tracksmith Eliot Ryder
description: Tracksmith's second shoe is a max-cushion easy-day cruiser: a 25mm drop-in ATPU midsole on a rockered 45mm platform, soft and bouncy but still stable, with gum rubber underfoot. Built for recovery jogs and relaxed long runs in classic preppy style. It has no interest in tempo work, and $220 is steep for a single-purpose trainer.
pros: Plush, bouncy ATPU cushioning that stays stable

name: Under Armour Infinite Elite
description: Under Armour's max-cushion flagship trainer with a thick HOVR+ supercritical midsole and a broad, stable platform. It is a plush cruiser for easy days and long runs, and its durable build suits bigger runners, though it carries noticeable weight.
pros: Stable base for a tall shoe
cons: Ride feels sluggish at faster paces

name: Under Armour Infinite Elite 2
description: UA's flagship HOVR+ max-cushion trainer, plush and protective for long easy days with a traditional 8mm drop. Suits heel-striking mileage grinders who want durable comfort from a non-specialist brand. At just over 10 oz it is not the pick for faster sessions.

name: Under Armour Infinite Mega
description: A premium UA x Speedland collab: a 43mm max-cushion road trainer with dual BOA dials over layered HOVR+ bead foam and supercritical EVA. A statement recovery/easy-day shoe for gearheads who value fit customization. At $250 and nearly 11 oz, it is niche and strictly for roads given the exposed midsole foam.
cons: Exposed foam limits it to pavement

name: Under Armour Infinite Pro
description: The mid-tier shoe in UA's Infinite line, with HOVR+ foam in a more moderate stack than the Elite for balanced everyday training. It is a comfortable, well-built daily trainer that competes on cushioning and durability rather than low weight.
pros: Balanced HOVR+ cushioning for daily miles
cons: A bit heavy versus similarly priced rivals
Nothing about the ride stands out

name: Under Armour Infinite Pro 2
description: A no-nonsense budget trainer with updated HOVR+ TPU-bead cushioning in an EVA carrier, built for dependable 4-7 mile daily runs. Good value for newer runners who want a secure fit and grippy outsole. It is heavy and unremarkable for long or fast efforts.
cons: Cushion feels basic beyond an hour

name: Under Armour Sonic 7
description: UA's entry-level HOVR road trainer with a low 26mm profile and a softer, lighter foam update; it won a 2025 Runner's World Shoe Award in the budget category. A sensible pick for beginners and short daily miles. Runners who want modern high-stack cushioning will find it thin.

name: Under Armour Velociti Elite 2
description: Under Armour's carbon-plated marathon racer, refining the shoe that carried Sharon Lokedi to a New York City Marathon win. It pairs a PEBA-based Flow midsole with a full carbon plate and UA's rubberless Flow outsole for a light, grippy, race-focused ride.
pros: Light with excellent road grip from the Flow outsole
cons: Super-shoe price from a challenger brand

name: Under Armour Velociti Elite 3
description: UA's carbon-plated marathon racer with a 37.5/35.5mm HOVR+ stack, a very pronounced rocker, and an unusually stable, broad platform for a super shoe. Best for midfoot strikers who like crisp rather than squishy energy return. The sharply tapered toe box and low 2mm drop will not suit everyone.
pros: More stable than most super shoes
